articles.title: Reverse Engineering the iPod Classic's Undocumented Mikey Chip
articles.summary: The iPod Classic's undocumented Mikey chip has no public documentation, with the only prior art being a 16-year-old reverse engineering writeup on a blog that no longer exists. The chip's event engine falls asleep after five seconds and reports button releases 1.8 seconds late, resulting in a driver that works for all three buttons. To fix the issue, a prebuilt Rockbox image with the remote driver is available, which can be downloaded and installed on an iPod in disk mode. Once the change is merged upstream, the official daily builds can be switched back.

articles.title: Alan Kay's answer to “Did the ENIAC have a BIOS”?
articles.summary: The ENIAC computer, built in the 1940s, had a firmware-based operating system, which was essentially a set of instructions that controlled the computer's hardware. Alan Kay, a pioneer in object-oriented programming, has long argued that the ENIAC's firmware-based system is a prime example of a "meta-os" - a layer of code that sits above the hardware and provides a higher-level interface for the computer. This concept is still relevant today, as it highlights the importance of understanding the underlying architecture of a system.

The author invites other library authors to review and provide feedback on a draft of the article, but retains editorial control. The project aims to address the instruction decoding bottleneck in CPUs by feeding the CPU a batch of numbers at once for a single arithmetic operation, a technique known as single instruction, multiple data or SIMD.
